common_name: Eglantyne Rose (Pure Pink Rounded Rosette David Austin Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Eglantyne bears clear soft pink, perfectly rounded rosette blooms on a compact, well-branched shrub.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Introduced by David Austin in 1994, Eglantyne bears pure, clear pink, fully double blooms in a neat, rounded rosette shape with a soft, sweet old-rose fragrance, one of the most classically pretty flower forms in the English rose line. Its compact, tidy, well-branched habit fits smaller beds and mixed borders without excessive size management. It reblooms in flushes from late spring through fall; prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood, and deadhead spent blooms through the season to sustain continued flowering.
sources: American Rose Society — English rose archive

common_name: Kew Gardens Rose (Floriferous White Single-Flowered Groundcover Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun; Kew Gardens is a low, wide-spreading, extremely floriferous Austin rose useful as a groundcover or low hedge.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Kew Gardens, a modern David Austin introduction, bears clusters of simple, single, pure white flowers with light fragrance in extraordinary profusion, covering its low, wide, spreading canes almost continuously from late spring through frost. Its groundcover-like habit and near-nonstop bloom make it useful as a low informal hedge, mass planting, or spilling over a low wall, a role quite different from the more upright, densely double-flowered roses typical of the English rose line. It shows good disease resistance for easier maintenance, and needs only light pruning in late winter to shape.
sources: American Rose Society — English rose archive

common_name: Lark Ascending Rose (Airy Apricot-Yellow Single-Flowered David Austin Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Lark Ascending is named for the Vaughan Williams composition and bears wild-rose-like single flowers on a tall, airy, upright shrub.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Introduced by David Austin in 2012 and named for the Vaughan Williams composition, Lark Ascending bears simple, single, apricot-yellow flowers with a light, fresh fragrance on a tall, upright, gracefully airy shrub, giving a naturalistic, wild-rose look quite different from the densely double blooms typical of most English roses. Its open flower form makes the stamens easily accessible to pollinators, and it reblooms reliably from late spring through fall. Prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood, and deadhead spent blooms through the season to sustain continued flowering.
sources: American Rose Society — English rose archive

common_name: Strawberry Hill Rose (Fragrant Rich Pink David Austin Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Strawberry Hill can be grown as a large shrub or trained as a short climber with a support.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Introduced by David Austin in 2006, Strawberry Hill bears large, cupped, richly petaled blooms in deep rose-pink with a strong myrrh fragrance, opening on long, arching canes vigorous enough to be trained as a short climber against a fence or pillar, or left to grow as a large informal shrub. It reblooms in strong flushes from late spring through fall. Prune to control size and shape in late winter — lightly if grown as a shrub, or by thinning old wood if trained as a climber — and deadhead spent blooms through the season to sustain continued flowering.
sources: American Rose Society — English rose archive

common_name: Gentle Hermione Rose (Intensely Fragrant Blush Pink David Austin Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Gentle Hermione is grown as much for its intense old-rose fragrance as for its soft blush-pink flowers.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Introduced by David Austin in 2005, Gentle Hermione bears soft blush-pink, cupped, rosette-shaped double flowers with one of the strongest and most admired fragrances in the entire English rose line, a rich, sweet old-rose scent that fills the surrounding air. Its compact, well-branched habit fits smaller beds and containers, and it reblooms reliably from late spring through fall. Prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood, and deadhead spent blooms through the season to sustain the long bloom season.
sources: American Rose Society — English rose archive

common_name: Young Lycidas Rose (Unusual Crimson-Purple Quartered David Austin Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Young Lycidas bears unusual crimson-purple, quartered, old-rose-form blooms with a fruity fragrance.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Introduced by David Austin in 2011, Young Lycidas bears an unusual crimson-purple flower color deepening toward true purple as blooms age, arranged in a neatly quartered, old-rose-style form reminiscent of antique Gallica roses, with a rich, fruity fragrance. Its distinctive coloring stands apart from the more common pinks and apricots of the English rose line, making it a striking accent among lighter-colored companions. It reblooms in flushes from late spring through fall; prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood, and deadhead spent blooms through the season.
sources: American Rose Society — English rose archive
